chapter_theme: Poems 301-320 move from the battle line to the warrior's house: horses and young riders, vows that frighten camps, a brahmin whose few words end a siege, warriors fallen with their elephants, and then the old houses and the able men of small villages, whose mothers assign duties, whose wives pray for guests at hero-stones, and whose lords pawn swords and promise gold to the bards.

301.reading: The speaker warns the many warriors in the thorn-fenced camp to guard their king and their elephants, for the hero opposite does not even go out to meet those who strike at him, no one knows what he intends, and having ridden off at night on his fine horse he looks like a man who will lift his spear only against the elephant the enemy king rides.
301.nuance: The threat lies in restraint: the hero's refusal to answer ordinary blows (எறிந்தோர் எதிர்சென்று எறிதலும் செல்லான்) is what makes him dangerous, because it shows he is saving his spear for the king's own elephant.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning across the battle line about one warrior's chosen target

comparisons.tenor: the thorn fence set round the camp
the short path the horseman rides, as if measuring the ground

302.reading: The horses leap and bound like a bamboo bursting; the village's flowers went to the women's hair and its narantham garlands to the bards; the poor small village on stony ground is never full, yet if one counted the elephants the young warrior killed with his spear they would outnumber the stars of the sky and the drops of the cool rain.
302.nuance: The poem sets the village's want (நிரம்பா இயல்பின் கரம்பைச் சீறூர்) against its giving: what little it has, flowers and garlands, has already gone to women and bards, and its only abundance is the count of its warrior's kills.

thinai_evidence.note: the count of elephants killed in battle

303.reading: A warrior speaks: the young rider who destroys his mockers is coming on a whirling horse that digs the ground with its hooves as if thrusting the earth back, to try his hot spear and scar the chest of me, who only yesterday, before famous kings, cut through their ranks like a boat through the sea and killed their tusked elephant so that its young cow mourned.
303.nuance: The colophon names the horse's valour, but the poem is spoken by the target: the older warrior describes the young rider's charge as a test he welcomes, and answers it with his own record of yesterday.

thinai_evidence.note: two warriors meeting in battle

comparisons.tenor: the horse's hooves tearing the ground
the speaker cutting through the kings' army

304.reading: The hero garlands the women, drinks strained toddy against the shivering cold, and hurries to harness his horse that outruns the wind; saying 'tomorrow I fight the younger brother of the man who escaped me yesterday', he will not even feed his lean belly but drives the strong horse hard, and when the victorious king's camp hears it, it trembles, because what he says does not come out two ways.
304.nuance: The enemy camp fears a sentence, not an army: its trembling rests on the hero's record that his word is never 'two' (இரண்டா காது), so the vow does the work of an assault.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's vow of battle and its effect on the enemy camp

305.reading: A lean, pale brahmin, his waist shrunk like a withered vayalai creeper, came at nightfall and went straight in; he spoke only a few words, and for them the siege ladders and the gate-bars were put away and the bells were taken off the well-trained war elephants.
305.nuance: The poem measures cause against effect: a frail man and a few words on one side, the whole apparatus of siege dismantled on the other; it never says what he said, which keeps the force on the brevity.

thinai_evidence.note: the brahmin's excellence is the war his words ended

306.reading: In a small village fenced with thorns that shake when elephants fight, where the well is hard to drink from, a woman with soft thick hair and bright brow worships the hero-stone with joined hands every day, praying that she may always have guests to receive and that her lord, [gap] with the king, may win a great war that brings land.
306.nuance: Her first request to the dead hero of the stone is guests, and only then her husband's war; hospitality and battle are asked of the same stone, and the war she wants is one that brings land (நாடுதரு), not one that merely brings fame.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman of a warrior house prays for guests and for her husband's war

307.reading: Where is my lord, our support? He fell with an elephant like a hill and lies like a stranger; see, the old ookam blossoms, like a summer squirrel's tail, settle on his long curled hair, and like a lame old bull the salt-carters abandoned without water or grass he still takes the lives of foes, so that the enemy king, seeing it, said there was nothing finer than to stay on this field and fell, his heart broken.
307.nuance: The image of the abandoned bull is pitiless: the support of the house (ஆசாகு எந்தை) lies like a beast left to die by a road, and yet the same lines give him the power to kill, so the lament and the boast share one figure.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior fallen with the elephant he killed

comparisons.tenor: the elephant the hero fell with
the fallen hero lying alone on the field

308.reading: A woman of the warrior house tells the bard with the gold-stringed little lute that the small-village chief's little-leafed spear now stands in the face of the king's mounted elephant, while the spear the angry king threw passed through the chests of those around her lord; and when our hero raised the bright weapon and drove forward, all the bull elephants turned their backs, to the shame of their young cows.
308.nuance: A small village's chief (சீறூர் மன்னன்) against a crowned king's elephants is the poem's proportion; the shame is transferred to the cow elephants, who watch their males flee.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed told is a battle against a king's elephants, though the colophon files it as an old house's pride

309.reading: Smashing iron-faced shields and crossing a great battle of foes is easy for anyone; what belongs to my lord is the single shining tall victorious spear at whose mere report 'he is in the camp' matchless enemies take fright, as people fear an anthill where a cobra lives or a common where a killing bull roams.
309.nuance: The poem demotes the deed the thurai names (cutting through the ranks) as common to all, and claims for the lord only the fear his presence causes; both similes are of a place made dangerous by what lives in it, not of the creature itself.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's valour judged in battle

comparisons.tenor: the camp where the lord is present
the camp where the lord is present

310.reading: Once, when milk was brought to him he would not drink, and he fretted at the little stick she raised without anger; now the son of the strong man who fell the other day, having killed a spotted elephant, says he does not even feel the arrow in his wound, as he lies on the shield, his tuft like a horse's mane, his beard just coming.
310.nuance: The before and after are both about refusing: the child who would not drink milk and feared a raised stick is now the youth who will not notice an arrow; the speaker's tenderness never says whether he lives.

thinai_evidence.note: a youth killing an elephant in battle

311.reading: Avvai speaks of a lord in a white cloth washed daily by the washerwoman in water from a well dug in saline ground, who sat in the pollen-strewn street and served the needs of many: in battle there is no one like him, the noble one who, when the honoured warriors' red eyes smoke with rage, covers them with his single shield.
311.nuance: The first half is all peace and humility: a plain washed cloth, sitting in the dust of the street, doing others' errands; the same man in battle is the one who hides others behind his shield, so his service does not change with the setting.

thinai_evidence.note: a hero praised for shielding others in battle

312.reading: To bear him and bring him up is my duty, to make him a worthy man is his father's, to forge and give him a spear is the smith's, to give him good conduct is the king's, and to cut through the hard battle with his shining sword, kill elephants and come back is the young man's duty.
312.nuance: Five duties are owed to the son by four givers, and the last, his own, is not to win but to return (பெயர்தல்) after killing elephants; the king's share is conduct (நன்னடை), not wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: a mother of a warrior house sets out each one's duty, ending in the son's

313.reading: The great hero of a land beside the wilderness has nothing in hand, yet if the suppliants who go longing to see him ask for elephants and tall chariots he is bound to give them; what he has in mind is as sure as the hill of salt the salt-carters with laden carts point to, without a sesame seed's doubt.
313.nuance: The word for his obligation is கடவ, 'bound to': giving is owed, not chosen, and the poem asserts it while saying in the same breath that he has nothing in his hand.

thinai_evidence.note: a chieftain's excellence in giving though he has nothing

314.reading: The husband of the bright-browed woman, a lamp to his house, the tall noble with the conquering spear who is the boundary of the battle front, is alone the stay of the people of the small village of thin-stemmed nelli on hard ground beside the leaf-strewn field of standing hero-stones, and if his own lord falls, he alone is the dam for the army that breaks rank and flees with its banners.
314.nuance: The three metaphors share one function at three scales: lamp to a house, boundary to a front, dam to a broken army; the village of hero-stones beside him shows what that function has cost others before him.

thinai_evidence.note: one man's excellence in house and in war

comparisons.tenor: the warrior who stops the routed army

315.reading: Avvai says of Neduman Anji: when he has, he can eat; he gives to suppliants even beyond those he is bound to; he is the joy and companion of simple folk; like the fire-drill stick tucked into the eaves of a house he can stay unseen, and like the roaring fire it gives off he can blaze out when he chooses to appear.
315.nuance: The two similes are one object in two states: the fire is already in the stick, so his restraint is not weakness but stored force, and the word வல்லன் (he can) is repeated for both eating, hiding and blazing.

thinai_evidence.note: a chieftain's excellence in giving and in timely force

comparisons.tenor: the patron when he shows his force

316.reading: The bard says: he who sleeps late in the yard overgrown with scrub, drowsy from the toddy he praises day after day, is our lord and we are his bards; yesterday he pawned his old iron-bound sword for guests who came, today this black-necked little lute is the pledge; do not think he has nothing to give, but take it, so that your slim-waisted woman may wear bright jewels and we may sway with our toddy pots, and may he go and come back red-mouthed when the king with small-eyed elephants meets trouble.
316.nuance: The pledge passes downward: the lord pawns his sword for guests, and the bard then offers his own lute as surety to the toddy-seller, so the household's credit rests on the lord's coming war, which will redeem both.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior who pawns his sword for guests and is ready for the king's war

317.reading: [Line 1 gapped] Whatever there is, a hide, a mat, anything, give it quickly to the great reveller lying in the front yard; [lines 5 and 6 gapped] having given to us, to others, to everyone, he took to sleep.
317.nuance: What survives is a reversal: the man who gave to everyone has nothing left to lie on, and the speaker asks others to give him a hide or a mat.

thinai_evidence.note: the gaps leave only the spear and the giving; the colophon's warrior excellence is followed

318.reading: The noble's town has gone hungry together with his dark woman of peacock grace, the plucked greens wilting and the gathered firewood drying unused; yet if the king meets trouble it becomes a place of plenty, where the house sparrow with its dark throat eats rice from the big fields and lives with its dull-backed hen in a nest woven of bards' lute-string fibres and plumes.
318.nuance: The village's plenty depends on its lord's distress turning into the warrior's opportunity (வேந்து விழுமுறின்): peace starves this house and war feeds it, so the sparrow's nest of bards' strings and plumes is a picture of the spoils to come.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior house whose plenty comes from the king's wars

319.reading: The wife of the small-village lord tells the old wise bard: the old jar in the yard of our small house, where a little reddish water from a well dug in red earth is poured, is clean and empty because we drank the toddy; it is too late to spread the millet out for the doves and quail; so though it is only roasted hare we will give it, come in and stay; our lord, whose boys yoke the trembling calf of the wild cow as if it were a calf of the house, went yesterday on the king's errand, and when he returns he will crown you with a lotus that never fades so that your paadini may wear a garland.
319.nuance: The wife offers what is gone (the toddy drunk, the millet unspread) before what she has (roasted hare), and pays the rest on credit against her husband's return: the unfading lotus is the gold the king's errand will bring.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's house receives a bard in his absence

comparisons.tenor: the wild cow's calf the boys yoke

320.reading: In a yard where munjai and musundai creepers make a shade no pandal is needed for, a hunter sleeps; a lone stag frolics with the tame decoy doe, and his wife, seeing their happy union, stays still, afraid her husband might wake and afraid the stag might leave the doe, while jungle fowl and quail noisily eat the millet drying on a deerskin; so, bard, eat the roasted meat smelling of sandal-fire with your whole kin, stay and then go, for this town is guarded by the famed noble who always gives the suppliants the fine food the king gives him.
320.nuance: A love scene sits inside a puram poem: the wife holds still between two fears, for her husband's sleep and for the deer's union, and lets the birds eat the household's millet rather than break either; the poem then turns the same open-handedness on the bard.

thinai_evidence.note: a hunter-warrior's town where the bard is fed

links.note: 301's hero will lift his spear only against the king's mounted elephant (வேந்தூர் யானைக்கு அல்லது); Kural 772 prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare.
links.teaches: The Kural states the warrior's preference for a worthy target as a maxim of honour, and 301 shows the same preference working as a tactic, since the enemy camp is warned that a man who ignores lesser blows is saving himself for their king.

links.note: Both kuthirai maram poems name the young rider with one formula: நோக்கினர்ச் செகுக்கும் காளை (302) and எள்ளுநர்ச் செகுக்கும் காளை (303).
links.teaches: The epithet for the young horseman was a fixed frame with a free slot for his victims, those who look at him or those who mock him, so two poets of the same thurai shared a stock line and varied only whom it threatened.

links.note: 303's speaker killed an elephant yesterday and now waits for a young rider's spear in his chest; Kural 774's warrior sends his spear off with an elephant and laughs as he pulls a spear from his own body.
links.teaches: Both pair the elephant killed with the spear received, so the couplet's laughing warrior is the same type as 303's boaster, and the poem supplies the couplet's missing sequence: the elephant was yesterday, the wound is today's test.

links.note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one said is hard; in 304 the king's camp trembles because the hero's word is never two (இரண்டா காது அவன் கூறியது).
links.teaches: The Kural treats word and deed as a gap to be closed by effort, but 304 shows a man whose record has closed it so firmly that his spoken vow alone frightens an army, so keeping one's word becomes a weapon and not only a virtue.

links.note: Kural 685 says the envoy speaks briefly and brings good; 305's brahmin says only a few words (சொல்லிய சொல்லோ சிலவே) and the siege ladders and elephants' bells are put away.
links.teaches: The couplet's rule for the envoy, brevity that achieves its end, has a historical scene behind it in which the good brought was a war called off, and the poem credits that to the words' fewness rather than to the speaker's power.

links.note: Kural 81 says all household life is for receiving guests; 306's woman prays at the hero-stone first that she may have guests (விருந்து எதிர் பெறுகதில்) and then for her husband's war.
links.teaches: The Kural's claim that household life exists for guests was a prayer before it was a maxim: in 306 a warrior's wife asks the hero-stone for guests before she asks for her husband's victory, so hospitality ranked first even in a house that lived by war.

links.note: Both set a small village (சீறூர்) beside hero-stones (நடுகல்): in 306 a woman worships the stone, in 314 the village of thin nelli stands by a field where stones rise.
links.teaches: Read together they show the hero-stone as part of the warrior village's daily setting, worshipped by the women and standing beside the living hero who is the village's stay, so the dead and the living defenders were kept in one view.

links.note: Kural 780 says a death that fills the patron's eyes with tears is worth begging for; in 307 the enemy king himself, seeing the fallen hero, says nothing is finer than to stay on this field.
links.teaches: The Kural measures a good death by the tears of one's own lord, while 307 goes further and makes the enemy king the witness who envies the death, so the honour of a field death did not depend on whose side mourned it.

links.note: Both name the king's mounted elephant as the warrior's chosen target with the same phrase: வேந்தூர் யானை (301 line 15) and வேந்துஊர் யானை (308 line 5).
links.teaches: The king's own elephant was the standard mark of a warrior's ambition, so 301's threat and 308's report are the before and after of one deed: the spear that 301 says is reserved for it is the spear 308 says now stands in its face.

links.note: Both are spoken by a follower of 'my lord' (என்னை): 309 says enemies fear at the report that he is in the camp, Kural 771 warns enemies not to stand before him, since many who did now stand as stones.
links.teaches: The Kural's chapter on martial pride keeps the Purananuru's speaking voice, the retainer boasting of என்னை, and 309 shows what the couplet compresses: the lord's power is the fear his name spreads before any blow, which is why the stones of 771 are the result rather than the boast.

links.note: In 279 a mother whose kin fell oils her only son's tuft (குடுமி) and sends him to battle; in 310 the son of a man who fell the other day lies on the shield with his tuft like a horse's mane after killing an elephant.
links.teaches: Together they form a sequence the anthology never states as one story: the boy sent out with oiled tuft after his father's death comes back to lie on the shield, so 310 shows the cost and the pride that 279's resolve was preparing.

links.note: Kural 67 says the father's duty is to make his son first in the assembly; 312 says the father's duty is to make him a worthy man (சான்றோன்) but the son's own duty is to kill elephants and return.
links.teaches: Both assign the father the son's standing among men, but 312 places that standing inside a chain of duties ending in war, so the 'worthy man' of a warrior house was finished by the battlefield, not by the assembly the Kural has in mind.

links.note: Kural 69 says the mother rejoices more to hear her son called சான்றோன் than at his birth; 312's mother says bearing him is her duty and making him சான்றோன் is the father's.
links.teaches: The same word marks the same two stages, birth and being called worthy, and 312 shows why the Kural's mother only hears of it: in this division of duties the worthiness is made by others, so her joy is at a work she began but did not finish.

links.note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not fail in obligation even when without means; 313's hero has nothing in hand yet is bound (கடவ) to give elephants and chariots to suppliants.
links.teaches: The couplet's abstract duty, giving even without means, is shown in 313 with its practical answer: a warrior without wealth gives what he will win, so the obligation was made possible by the economy of plunder the Kural does not mention.

links.note: Kural 1027 likens the one who carries the family's burden to the stout-hearted in battle; 314 shows one man as lamp of his house and dam of the routed army.
links.teaches: The Kural uses the battle hero as a simile for the family's mainstay, while 314 shows that in the warrior village they were literally the same man, so the couplet's comparison grew from a social fact that it turned into a figure.

links.note: Kural 490 says to fold up like the heron when it is time and strike like its beak when the moment comes; 315 says Anji can stay unseen like the fire-drill in the eaves and blaze like its fire when he appears.
links.teaches: Both reduce right timing to one object with two states, but Avvai's image puts the force inside the waiting thing (the fire is already in the stick), which adds to the couplet that restraint is stored strength rather than mere patience.

links.note: Kural 926 says sleepers are like the dead and toddy-drinkers eat poison; 316 praises as 'our lord' a man asleep in a drunken drowse who pawns his sword for guests.
links.teaches: On the plain reading the two judge the same figure oppositely, since the drunken sleeper whom the Kural calls as good as dead is in 316 the generous lord of the bards, which shows that the Kural's ban on drink rejects a heroic ideal the Sangam village celebrated.

links.note: Both show a drinking warrior at rest in his front yard (சீயா முன்றில் in 316, முன்றில் கிடந்த பெருங்களியாளற்கு in 317) after giving everything away.
links.teaches: The two consecutive poems share a portrait, the reveller who has given away his sword or his bedding, which suggests the vallaan mullai thurai had a stock figure in whom poverty, drink and open-handedness were marks of the same character.

links.note: Kural 89 calls neglect of guests poverty in the midst of wealth; in 319 the wife, with an empty jar and only roasted hare, takes in the bard and promises a golden lotus on her husband's return.
links.teaches: The couplet defines the failure, poverty inside wealth, and 319 shows its converse, generosity inside poverty, where what is lacking is paid on credit against the husband's next war, so hospitality was measured by readiness to give, not by stores.

links.note: Both invite a bard to stay in a warrior's small house and eat game (முயல் in 319, வள்ளூரம் in 320), with ஈங்குஇருந் தீமோ in 319 and தங்கினை சென்மோ, பாண in 320.
links.teaches: Read together they give the vallaan mullai poem's fixed shape, a description of the poor or wild household, an offer of roasted game, and a closing pledge of the lord's giving, so the bard's welcome was a set form that each poet filled with his own scene.

links.note: 320 lines 17 and 18 and 329 lines 8 and 9 are the same: அருகாது ஈயும் வண்மை / உரைசால் நெடுந்தகை ஓம்பும் ஊரே.
links.teaches: The two poems end on an identical couplet after different openings, a hunter's yard and a village by the hero-stones, which shows that the closing praise of the town's guardian was a detachable formula the poets set after their own scenes.

source_issues: 302: the poet field carries an editor's variant note, வெறிபாடிய காமக் கண்ணியார் (காமக் கணியார் எனவும் பாடம்); copied as it stands.

306: line 6 is gapped after its first letter (ஒ .. ..), so the prayer for the husband is incomplete; the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1, which the poem needs (its fence and elephants set the village).
310, 314, 315, 316, 318: the review lists these among our poems with stray non-Tamil glyphs; the text as `show` prints it was read as it stands.
312: the poet, thinai and thurai are filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition (FILLED_FROM_DURAISAMY_PILLAI); this poem is usually attributed with 310 to Ponmudiyar, as here.
313, 314, 315: the colophon thurai reads வல்லான் முல்லை; 316 to 320 read வல்லாண் முல்லை, the usual name; normalised to வல்லாண்முல்லை in puram_thurai.
317: lines 1, 5 and 6 are largely lost to gaps; the poet field reads மவேம்ப்ற்றூர்க் குமரனார், apparently a misprint for வேம்பற்றூர்க் குமரனார்.
319: line 4 reads கஃடு, read here as the toddy (கள்) that was drunk; lines 6 and 7 are hard to construe.
320: lines 17 and 18 repeat 329 lines 8 and 9 exactly (flag repeated_line).
